sections.h2: How does an eviction work in Maine?
sections.html:
A Maine landlord must give a written notice, then file a court case, then win a judgment, then wait for a writ of possession that a sheriff or constable serves. Maine calls the court case a forcible entry and detainer action, or FED, and 14 M.R.S. Chapter 709 governs it.

Each step has strict paperwork. A defective notice or a missed service step can reset the clock. If you own a rented house and are thinking about selling, it helps to know where the case stands, because the stage it has reached decides what a buyer can do.

This page uses the statutes and the Maine Judicial Branch's self-help guide for rent cases. It is general information, not legal advice.

sections.h2: Which notice does a Maine landlord have to serve first?
sections.html:
It depends on why the tenancy is ending. For a tenancy at will, 14 M.R.S. §6002 allows either side to end it with at least 30 days' written notice, and a 7-day notice for specific grounds.

NoticeWhen it is usedKey rule
30-day noticeEnding a tenancy at will without a stated faultMust tell the tenant of the right to contest in court; if rent is paid past the 30 days, the notice must expire on or after that date
7-day noticeRent 7 or more days in arrears, nuisance, substantial damage not repaired, unauthorized occupant, and certain violence-related groundsMust state the specific ground; a rent notice must state the amount owed and the cure statement

The statute lets a landlord combine a 30-day and a 7-day notice in one document. A clerical error in the arrears figure does not void the notice if it was unintentional and does not materially change its purpose. Starting January 1, 2024, landlords must also attach the judicial branch's form notice to termination notices, under 14 M.R.S. §6001.

sections.h2: How does a tenant stop an eviction for unpaid rent?
sections.html:
By paying. If the tenant pays the full rent due before a 7-day arrears notice expires, the notice is void. After it expires, paying all arrears, rent due and the filing and service fees before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy, and no writ may issue.

Payment or written assurance of payment through the general assistance program counts as cash for this purpose. That matters to a landlord planning a sale, because a nonpayment case can end suddenly when rent arrives.

A tenant can also raise the implied warranty of habitability in a nonpayment case. The landlord must have had actual or constructive notice of the problem and unreasonably failed to make repairs, and the tenant must not have caused it. If the court finds the unit unfit, the tenant owes only reduced fair rental value until repairs are made. The habitability duty itself appears in 14 M.R.S. §6021, which also covers heat and mold.

sections.h2: What are the court steps and costs for a rent case?
sections.html:
The Maine Judicial Branch lays out a seven-step path in its guide to evicting a tenant for not paying rent.

  1. Serve a 7-day notice to quit under §6002(1), with the information sheet (form CV-256).
  2. Prepare the complaint (CV-007), summons (CV-034, $5 each from the clerk) and the other required forms. List all tenants and add "and all other occupants" if others live there.
  3. Serve the papers through the county sheriff only after the notice period ends.
  4. File the notice to quit, the complaint, the summons with the return of service and the lease, with a $100 filing fee, before the hearing.
  5. Attend the hearing even if the tenant does not. Mediation is available at the court that day at no extra cost.
  6. If you win, you receive a judgment for possession and a writ of possession.
  7. If the tenant has not left, buy the writ from the clerk and hire a sheriff to serve it.

The guide says eviction does not collect back rent. That requires a separate case, often in Small Claims Court. Where a tenant cannot be served in hand after three good-faith attempts on three different days, 14 M.R.S. §6004 permits first-class mail plus leaving a copy at the tenant's last and usual residence, with an affidavit filed.

sections.h2: How long does a tenant have after the judgment?
sections.html:
The court issues the writ of possession seven calendar days after judgment is entered. After a sheriff or constable serves it, the tenant has 48 hours to leave, under 14 M.R.S. §6005.

A tenant who stays past 48 hours is treated as a trespasser, and the belongings are considered abandoned under §6013. No writ issues if the tenancy ended for rent arrears and the tenant paid the amount needed to reinstate.

An appeal can slow things. Under §6008, either party may appeal to Superior Court, and a defendant who appeals must pay the lesser of the unpaid current month's rent or the arrearage. The court can stay the writ on conditions such as continued rent payments. The deadline is the earlier of the writ's issuance or 30 days after judgment.

sections.h2: What happens to a tenant's belongings after an eviction?
sections.html:
The landlord must store them in a safe, dry, secured location and send written notice by first-class mail with proof of mailing. 14 M.R.S. §6013 sets out the timing.

  • The notice must include an itemized list of the items and containers.
  • The tenant has 7 days from the notice to claim the property.
  • If the tenant responds, the landlord must keep storing it for at least 14 days after sending the notice.
  • If the tenant claims the property within 7 days, release cannot be conditioned on fees or other amounts owed.
  • For unclaimed property, the landlord may sell it at a reasonable fair market price. Proceeds go first to back rent, damages and costs, and any balance goes to the Treasurer of State.

sections.h2: What can stop or delay an eviction?
sections.html:
Several defenses are written into the statute. Section 6001 creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation if, within 6 months before the action, the tenant asserted listed statutory rights, complained in good faith about code violations, made written repair requests or filed fair housing complaints. A writ cannot issue without rebuttal.

  • A tenant may raise a landlord's failure to provide a reasonable accommodation for a disability.
  • Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking cannot be evicted for those incidents.
  • A bona fide tenancy in a building with a pending foreclosure may be ended only under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009.
  • A new owner or assignee generally cannot bring the process against a tenant at will unless that tenant received proper notice under §6002.

sections.h2: What happens to a Maine rental when the owner sells?
sections.html:
Security deposits must be accounted for and transferred no later than the real estate closing. 14 M.R.S. §6035 says the holder of the deposits, including the landlord, agent or executor, must either transfer them to the successor with an accounting or return them to the tenants.

  • The seller mails each tenant notice of the transfer, the new owner's name and address, and a copy of the accounting.
  • At closing, the seller gives the buyer written proof of the accounting and transfer.
  • Once the holder complies, it is relieved of further liability for those funds, and the buyer takes the same duties as a landlord.
  • Under §6038, deposits must be kept in a bank account protected from the landlord's creditors, and a tenant can recover the greater of actual damages, $500 or one month's rent for a violation.

A tenant with a lease generally stays through a sale, because the buyer steps into the landlord's place. A buyer who wants the house empty has to wait for the lease to end or follow the notice rules above.

sections.h2: Should you evict first or sell the house with tenants in place?
sections.html:
It depends on timing and cost. An eviction can take weeks, adds filing and sheriff fees, and ends with a unit that may need work. Selling with tenants avoids that, but the buyer must accept the lease and the deposit transfer.

We buy Maine houses with tenants, unpaid rent or deferred repairs, as-is. A cash sale lets you hand off the property without waiting for a court date. If you are in the middle of a case, talk to a Maine attorney before you sign anything, and make sure the closing includes the deposit accounting that §6035 requires.

faqs.q: How long does a Maine eviction take?
faqs.a: It depends on the notice period, the hearing date and whether the tenant appeals. The fixed pieces are a 7-day or 30-day notice, a writ issued 7 calendar days after judgment, and 48 hours for the tenant to leave once the writ is served.

faqs.q: How much notice does a Maine landlord have to give?
faqs.a: At least 30 days' written notice to end a tenancy at will, or a 7-day notice for grounds such as rent 7 or more days late, nuisance or substantial damage. A lease may add its own terms.

faqs.q: What is the filing fee for an eviction in Maine?
faqs.a: The Maine Judicial Branch's guide for rent cases lists a $100 filing fee, plus $5 for each summons from the clerk. Writ and sheriff service fees are separate.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Maine while the tenant is still there?
faqs.a: Yes. The tenant's lease generally continues with the new owner. At closing the seller must transfer or return security deposits, give the buyer written proof, and mail each tenant notice of the transfer.
No. The court's guide says eviction does not collect back rent. That requires a separate case, often in Small Claims Court.

faqs.q: What if the tenant pays after getting a 7-day notice?
faqs.a: Paying all rent due before the notice expires voids it. Paying all arrears and filing and service fees after expiration but before the writ issues reinstates the tenancy, and no writ may issue.
